questions.question: How many fundamental quantities are there in the SI system?
questions.explanation: SI defines seven base quantities: length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental SI quantity?
questions.explanation: Force is a derived quantity (F = ma); the other three are SI base quantities.

questions.question: Which of these is a derived quantity?
questions.explanation: Energy = force × distance, derived from base quantities.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement of a good unit?
questions.explanation: A good unit is invariable — independent of temperature, pressure or location.

questions.question: Every measurement must include a numerical value AND a unit.
questions.explanation: A bare number with no unit conveys no measurement information.

questions.question: The international system of units used in physics is abbreviated ____.
questions.explanation: SI = Système International d'unités (International System of Units).

questions.question: The SI base unit of mass is the:
questions.explanation: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).

questions.question: The SI base unit of electric current is the:
questions.explanation: The SI base unit of electric current is the ampere (A); coulomb is derived (A·s).

questions.question: The SI unit of force is the:
questions.explanation: Newton (N) = kg·m/s² is the derived SI unit of force.

questions.question: The SI unit of pressure is the:
questions.explanation: Pascal (Pa) = N/m² is the SI unit of pressure.

questions.question: The SI unit of energy is the:
questions.explanation: Joule (J) = N·m = kg·m²/s² is the SI unit of energy and work.

questions.question: The SI unit of power is the:
questions.explanation: Watt (W) = J/s is the SI unit of power.

questions.question: 1 nanometre equals:
questions.explanation: Prefix nano means 10⁻⁹.

questions.question: 1 GHz is the same as:
questions.explanation: Prefix giga (G) = 10⁹.

questions.question: 1 watt is equal to 1 joule per second.
questions.explanation: Power is energy per unit time; 1 W = 1 J/s.

questions.question: 1 micrometre = 10^____ metre.
questions.explanation: Prefix micro = 10⁻⁶.

questions.question: How many seconds are there in 1 nanosecond?
questions.explanation: 1 ns = 10⁻⁹ s by definition of the prefix nano.

questions.question: Convert 5 kJ into joules.
questions.explanation: Prefix kilo = 10³, so 5 kJ = 5 × 10³ J = 5000 J.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of velocity is:
questions.explanation: Velocity is length / time, so [L T⁻¹].

questions.question: The dimensional formula of acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration = velocity / time = (L T⁻¹)/T = L T⁻².

questions.question: The dimensional formula of force is:
questions.explanation: F = m·a → mass × (L T⁻²) → [M L T⁻²].

questions.question: The dimensional formula of energy / work is:
questions.explanation: Energy = force × distance = (M L T⁻²)·L = M L² T⁻².

questions.question: The dimensional formula of power is:
questions.explanation: Power = energy / time = (M L² T⁻²)/T = M L² T⁻³.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of pressure is:
questions.explanation: Pressure = force / area = (M L T⁻²) / L² = M L⁻¹ T⁻².

questions.question: Two physical quantities have the same dimensions. They:
options: can be added or subtracted directly
must have the same numerical value
questions.answer: can be added or subtracted directly
questions.explanation: Dimensional homogeneity: only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or equated. Same dimensions does NOT mean same quantity (e.g. work and torque both have [M L² T⁻²]).

questions.question: Every term in a physically valid equation must have the same dimensions.
questions.explanation: This is the principle of dimensional homogeneity.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of momentum (p = mv) is [M L T^____].
questions.explanation: p = mv → kg·(m/s) → [M L T⁻¹].

questions.question: Check by dimensional analysis whether the equation v² = u² + 2as is consistent (v, u are velocities, a is acceleration, s is displacement).
options: Inconsistent — different dimensions on the two sides
Consistent — every term has dimensions [L² T⁻²]
Consistent — every term has dimensions [L T⁻¹]
Cannot be checked without numerical values
questions.answer: Consistent — every term has dimensions [L² T⁻²]
questions.explanation: [v²] = [u²] = (LT⁻¹)² = L²T⁻²; [2as] = (LT⁻²)·L = L²T⁻². All three terms match.

questions.question: Using dimensional analysis, the period T of a simple pendulum can depend on its length L and gravitational acceleration g. What does T equal (up to a dimensionless constant)?
questions.explanation: Assume T = k L^a g^b. [T] = [L]^a [LT⁻²]^b = L^(a+b) T^(−2b). Match T¹ → −2b = 1 → b = −1/2. Match L⁰ → a + b = 0 → a = 1/2. So T ∝ √(L/g).

questions.question: Which of the following is a TRUE limitation of dimensional analysis?
options: It cannot detect missing dimensionless constants like 2π or ½
It cannot check the units of an equation
It works only for SI units
It cannot distinguish length from area
questions.answer: It cannot detect missing dimensionless constants like 2π or ½
questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis fixes dimensions but not numerical factors. It also cannot detect missing terms with the same dimensions or determine functional forms like sin(x), exp(x).

questions.question: Why does dimensional analysis fail to determine the equation s = ut + (1/2) a t²?
options: The equation is not dimensionally consistent.
Dimensional analysis cannot find the dimensionless coefficient 1/2.
The equation has more than one term.
Dimensional analysis cannot detect the term (1/2) at all.
questions.answer: Dimensional analysis cannot find the dimensionless coefficient 1/2.
questions.explanation: All terms in s = ut + (1/2)at² have dimensions of length, so the equation is consistent; the 1/2 is a dimensionless constant that dimensional analysis cannot determine.

questions.question: How many significant figures are there in the measurement 24.50 cm?
questions.explanation: Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 2, 4, 5, 0 → 4 sig figs.

questions.question: How many significant figures are there in 0.00250?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are NOT significant; 2, 5, 0 → 3 sig figs.

questions.question: How many significant figures are in 6.022 × 10²³?
questions.explanation: In scientific notation, only the digits in the mantissa count: 6, 0, 2, 2 → 4 sig figs.

questions.question: When multiplying or dividing measurements, the result should have:
options: the same number of decimal places as the most precise input
the same number of significant figures as the least precise input
the same number of significant figures as the most precise input
as many digits as you want
questions.answer: the same number of significant figures as the least precise input
questions.explanation: Multiplication / division → match sig-figs to the least precise input.

questions.question: When adding measurements, the answer is rounded to the smallest number of decimal places among the inputs.
questions.explanation: Addition / subtraction rule: match decimal places (not sig-figs) to the least precise input.

questions.question: 12.5 + 0.025 = ____ (rounded correctly).
questions.explanation: 12.5 has 1 decimal place; 12.525 rounds to 12.5.

questions.question: Errors that always shift readings in one direction (e.g. a miscalibrated instrument) are called:
questions.explanation: Systematic errors are repeatable and biased; calibration error is the textbook example.

questions.question: Errors caused by uncontrolled variations from one measurement to the next are called:
questions.explanation: Random errors fluctuate in both directions; averaging reduces them.

questions.question: Random errors can be reduced (but not eliminated) by:
options: using a more precise instrument scale alone
looking only at the first reading
questions.explanation: Random errors fluctuate; their average tends to zero as the number of measurements grows.

questions.question: If the mean value of a quantity is x̄ and the mean absolute error is Δx, the relative error is:
questions.explanation: Relative error = mean absolute error / mean value (dimensionless). Percentage error = 100 × Δx / x̄.

questions.question: If z = x · y, the relative error in z is:
questions.explanation: Relative errors in products and quotients add.

questions.question: If z = x ± y, the absolute error in z (worst case) is:
questions.explanation: Absolute errors add for sums and differences (worst-case combination).

questions.question: If z = x⁵, the relative error in z is approximately:
questions.explanation: For z = xⁿ, relative error in z = n · (relative error in x).

questions.question: If a length is measured as 25.4 ± 0.2 cm, the percentage error is approximately ____ %.
questions.explanation: Percentage error = (0.2 / 25.4) × 100 ≈ 0.79%.

questions.question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and direction; the others are scalars.

questions.question: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Energy is fully specified by a number with units; force, velocity and torque are vectors.

questions.question: Two vectors are equal if and only if:
options: they have the same magnitude AND the same direction
they share the same starting point
questions.answer: they have the same magnitude AND the same direction
questions.explanation: Vectors are determined by magnitude and direction; the position of the tail does not matter.

questions.question: A vector of magnitude 1 is called a:
questions.explanation: Unit vector: magnitude exactly 1, used to specify direction.

questions.question: Vectors that lie in the same plane are called:
questions.explanation: Coplanar vectors share a common plane; collinear share a common line.

questions.question: The magnitude of a vector can be negative.
questions.explanation: Magnitude is always non-negative; direction encodes the sign information.

questions.question: The unit vector along the +x axis is denoted ____.
questions.explanation: Standard right-handed Cartesian basis: î, ĵ, k̂ along x, y, z.

questions.question: Which of these is the negative of the vector \vec{a} = 3î + 4ĵ?
questions.explanation: Negative reverses every component: \vec{a} = (3, 4) → −\vec{a} = (−3, −4).

questions.question: What is the magnitude of \vec{a} = 3î + 4ĵ?
What is the magnitude of \vec{a} = 6î − 8ĵ?
When two vectors are added by the parallelogram law, the resultant is the:
options: diagonal that starts at the common tail
questions.answer: diagonal that starts at the common tail
questions.explanation: The resultant runs along the diagonal that begins at the common starting point of the two vectors.

questions.question: Two vectors of magnitude 3 and 4 act at right angles. The magnitude of their sum is:
Two vectors of magnitudes 5 and 3 point in the same direction. The magnitude of their sum is:
questions.explanation: Same direction → resultant magnitude = 5 + 3 = 8 (cos 0 = 1).

questions.question: Two vectors of magnitudes 5 and 3 point in opposite directions. The magnitude of their sum is:
questions.explanation: Opposite directions → magnitude of sum = |5 − 3| = 2.

questions.question: If \vec{a} = 2î + 3ĵ and \vec{b} = 4î − ĵ, find \vec{a} + \vec{b}.
questions.explanation: Add components: (2 + 4)î + (3 + (−1))ĵ = 6î + 2ĵ.

questions.question: If \vec{a} = 5î + 12ĵ, find a unit vector along \vec{a}.
The dot product \vec{a} · \vec{b} equals:
questions.explanation: Definition: \vec{a} · \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| cos θ where θ is the angle between them.

questions.question: The cross product \vec{a} × \vec{b} has magnitude:
questions.explanation: |\vec{a} × \vec{b}| = a b sin θ, with direction perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule.

questions.question: The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is:
questions.explanation: cos 90° = 0, so \vec{a} · \vec{b} = a b cos 90° = 0.

questions.question: The cross product of two parallel vectors is:
questions.explanation: sin 0 = 0, so |\vec{a} × \vec{b}| = 0; the cross product is the zero vector.

questions.question: If \vec{a} = 2î + 3ĵ and \vec{b} = î − ĵ, compute \vec{a} · \vec{b}.
If \vec{F} = 4î + 3ĵ N and the displacement is \vec{d} = 2î + 0ĵ m, the work done is:
If two vectors of magnitudes 6 and 8 are perpendicular, the magnitude of their cross product is:
questions.explanation: |\vec{a} × \vec{b}| = a b sin θ = 6 × 8 × sin 90° = 48.

questions.question: The cross product is anti-commutative: \vec{a} × \vec{b} = −\vec{b} × \vec{a}.
questions.explanation: Reversing the order reverses the direction of the resulting vector.

questions.question: The torque \vec{τ} of a force \vec{F} applied at position \vec{r} is given by ____.
questions.explanation: Torque is the cross product of position vector and force.

questions.question: Which two of the following pairs of physical quantities have the SAME dimensional formula?
questions.explanation: Both work and torque have dimensions [M L² T⁻²]. The other pairs differ in dimensions.

questions.question: Find the dimensions of universal gravitational constant G in F = G m₁m₂ / r².
questions.explanation: G = F r² / (m₁ m₂); [G] = (M L T⁻²)·L² / M² = M⁻¹ L³ T⁻².

questions.question: Two vectors of equal magnitude make an angle of 60° between them. The magnitude of their resultant is:
The angle between vectors \vec{a} = î + ĵ and \vec{b} = î − ĵ is:
questions.explanation: \vec{a} · \vec{b} = (1)(1) + (1)(−1) = 0 → vectors are perpendicular.

questions.question: Two equal-magnitude vectors must give zero resultant when:
options: they are parallel and same direction
questions.explanation: \vec{a} + (−\vec{a}) = 0; only the antiparallel case (θ = 180°) gives a zero resultant for equal-magnitude vectors.

questions.question: Dimensional analysis can determine whether the equation x = A sin(ωt + φ) is correct.
questions.explanation: The argument of sin must be dimensionless (so ωt is dimensionless), but dimensional analysis alone cannot determine the sin functional form or its constants.

questions.question: Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
The dimensional formula of frequency is:
questions.explanation: Frequency = 1/period; [Hz] = 1/s = T⁻¹.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of charge is:
questions.explanation: Charge = current × time; SI: A · s, dimensions [A T].

questions.question: The number 2.0 × 10⁴ has:
questions.explanation: Only the digits in the mantissa count: 2 and 0 → 2 sig figs.

questions.question: The number 1200 written with 2 significant figures in scientific notation is ____ × 10³.
questions.explanation: 1.2 × 10³ has exactly 2 sig figs.

questions.question: The position vector of a point P(3, 4, 0) is:
questions.explanation: 3î + 4ĵ + 0k̂ is the same vector as 3î + 4ĵ; the zero z-component is dropped by convention.

questions.question: What is î · î ?
questions.explanation: Dot product of a unit vector with itself: 1 · 1 · cos 0° = 1.

questions.question: What is î · ĵ ?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular unit vectors → dot product is 0.

questions.question: What is î × ĵ ?
questions.explanation: By the right-hand rule on the standard basis: î × ĵ = k̂.

questions.question: What is ĵ × î ?
questions.explanation: Anti-commutativity: ĵ × î = −(î × ĵ) = −k̂.

questions.question: Compute (2î + 3ĵ) × (î + ĵ).
If \vec{a} · \vec{b} = 0 and neither vector is zero, the vectors must be perpendicular.
questions.explanation: a b cos θ = 0 with a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0 forces cos θ = 0, i.e. θ = 90°.

questions.question: The dot product of two vectors is itself a vector.
questions.explanation: The dot product is a scalar (just a number).

questions.question: If two vectors are antiparallel, the angle between them is ____ degrees.
questions.explanation: Antiparallel = pointing in exactly opposite directions, θ = 180°.

questions.question: If x = 4.0 ± 0.1 cm and y = 2.0 ± 0.1 cm, the percentage error in z = x · y is approximately:
The radius of a sphere is measured as 2.00 ± 0.01 cm. The percentage error in the volume V = (4/3)πr³ is approximately:
Two forces of magnitudes 5 N and 12 N act at right angles on a body. The magnitude of the resultant force is:
If \vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = 0 and a = 3, b = 5, c = 7, the angle between \vec{a} and \vec{b} is:
questions.explanation: \vec{c} = −(\vec{a} + \vec{b}); |c|² = a² + b² + 2 a b cos θ → 49 = 9 + 25 + 30 cos θ → cos θ = 15/30 = 1/2 → θ = 60°.

questions.question: List the seven SI base units along with the physical quantity each represents.
questions.answer: Length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s); electric current: ampere (A); thermodynamic temperature: kelvin (K); amount of substance: mole (mol); luminous intensity: candela (cd).

questions.question: Check by dimensional analysis whether the equation v = u + a t² is dimensionally consistent (v, u: velocity, a: acceleration, t: time). Justify.
questions.answer: [v] = LT⁻¹; [u] = LT⁻¹; [a t²] = (LT⁻²)(T²) = L. The first two terms have dimensions LT⁻¹ but a t² has dimensions L. The dimensions of the three terms do NOT match, so the equation is dimensionally inconsistent and therefore cannot be physically correct.

questions.question: Derive, by dimensional analysis, how the period T of a simple pendulum depends on its length L and the acceleration due to gravity g (up to a dimensionless constant).
questions.answer: Assume T = k L^a g^b. Match dimensions: [T] = T¹; [L^a g^b] = L^a · (LT⁻²)^b = L^(a+b) T^(−2b). Equate exponents: T → −2b = 1 → b = −1/2. L → a + b = 0 → a = 1/2. So T ∝ L^(1/2) g^(−1/2) = √(L/g). The dimensionless constant (which dimensional analysis cannot fix) is 2π.

questions.question: State three limitations of dimensional analysis.
questions.answer: (1) It cannot determine dimensionless constants (like 2π or 1/2). (2) It cannot detect missing terms that have the same dimensions as the kept terms — only the homogeneity of present terms can be checked. (3) It cannot determine functional forms — equations involving sin(x), cos(x), exp(x), log(x) have arguments that must be dimensionless, but dimensional analysis alone cannot derive them.

questions.question: State the rules for significant figures in (i) multiplication / division and (ii) addition / subtraction. Give one numerical example for each.
questions.answer: (i) Multiplication / division: the result has the same number of sig figs as the input with the fewest sig figs. Example: 3.45 × 2.0 = 6.9 (2 sig figs, matching 2.0). (ii) Addition / subtraction: the result has the same number of decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places. Example: 12.45 + 1.2 = 13.65 → reported as 13.7 (one decimal place, matching 1.2).

questions.question: Distinguish systematic and random errors with one example each.
questions.answer: Systematic error: a repeatable, biased deviation from the true value, always in the same direction. Example: a stopwatch that runs 0.5 s slow always under-reads time. Random error: an unpredictable fluctuation from one measurement to the next. Example: variation in reaction time when starting and stopping a stopwatch by hand. Systematic errors are reduced by calibration; random errors are reduced by averaging many measurements.

questions.question: If x = 5.0 ± 0.1 m and y = 2.0 ± 0.05 m, find the absolute and percentage errors in z = x + y.
questions.answer: z = 5.0 + 2.0 = 7.0 m. Absolute errors add for sums: Δz = Δx + Δy = 0.1 + 0.05 = 0.15 m. Percentage error = (Δz / z) × 100 = (0.15 / 7.0) × 100 ≈ 2.14%. So z = 7.0 ± 0.15 m, ≈ 2.14% error.

questions.question: Distinguish a scalar from a vector quantity, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: A scalar is fully specified by a magnitude and a unit; it has no direction. Examples: mass (5 kg), temperature (298 K), energy, time. A vector is specified by both a magnitude and a direction. Examples: displacement (5 m east), force (10 N upward), velocity, momentum, electric field.

questions.question: Resolve a vector of magnitude 10 m at 60° above the +x axis into x- and y-components.
questions.answer: Magnitude a = 10 m, angle θ = 60°. Components: a_x = a cos θ = 10 × cos 60° = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m. a_y = a sin θ = 10 × sin 60° = 10 × (√3/2) ≈ 8.66 m. So \vec{a} = 5 î + 8.66 ĵ m.

questions.question: Compute the dot product and the angle between \vec{a} = 3 î + 4 ĵ and \vec{b} = 4 î − 3 ĵ.
questions.answer: \vec{a} · \vec{b} = (3)(4) + (4)(−3) = 12 − 12 = 0. Magnitudes: |\vec{a}| = √(9 + 16) = 5; |\vec{b}| = √(16 + 9) = 5. cos θ = (\vec{a} · \vec{b}) / (|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|) = 0 / 25 = 0, so θ = 90°. The vectors are perpendicular.

questions.question: Two forces of 10 N and 6 N act on a body, with a 60° angle between them. Find the magnitude of the resultant.
questions.answer: |R| = √(F₁² + F₂² + 2 F₁ F₂ cos θ) = √(100 + 36 + 2·10·6·cos 60°) = √(136 + 120·(1/2)) = √(136 + 60) = √196 = 14 N. So the resultant has magnitude 14 N.

questions.question: (a) State the principle of dimensional homogeneity. (b) Use dimensional analysis to check whether the equation T = 2π √(L/g) is dimensionally correct (T: time, L: length, g: acceleration). (c) State which dimensionless constant is fixed by physics rather than dimensions in this case.
questions.answer: (a) Principle of dimensional homogeneity: in any physically valid equation, every term must have the same dimensions; equivalently, the dimensions of the LHS must equal the dimensions of the RHS. (b) [T] on the LHS is T. On the RHS, [√(L/g)] = √(L / LT⁻²) = √(T²) = T. The 2π is dimensionless. So both sides have dimensions T — the equation is dimensionally consistent. (c) The constant 2π is dimensionless and is determined by the actual physics (solving the differential equation of small-angle pendulum motion), not by dimensional analysis.

questions.question: Two vectors are given by \vec{a} = 2 î + 3 ĵ − k̂ and \vec{b} = î − 2 ĵ + 4 k̂. (a) Find \vec{a} + \vec{b} and \vec{a} − \vec{b}. (b) Compute \vec{a} · \vec{b} and the angle between them. (c) Compute \vec{a} × \vec{b}.

Five measurements of the length of a rod are 25.5, 25.6, 25.4, 25.5, 25.5 cm. Compute (a) the mean value, (b) the mean absolute error, (c) the relative error, and (d) the percentage error. Express the result as length ± Δ length.
(a) State the right-hand rule for the cross product \vec{a} × \vec{b}. (b) Show by computation that î × ĵ = k̂ but ĵ × î = −k̂, and explain why this anti-commutativity is consistent with the rule.
questions.answer: (a) Right-hand rule: orient the right hand so that the fingers curl from \vec{a} toward \vec{b} through the smaller angle; the extended thumb points along \vec{a} × \vec{b}. (b) î × ĵ: |î × ĵ| = (1)(1)sin 90° = 1; the thumb (when fingers curl from î (x) to ĵ (y)) points along +z, so î × ĵ = k̂. ĵ × î: same magnitude 1; now fingers curl from ĵ (y) to î (x), so the thumb points along −z, giving ĵ × î = −k̂. Anti-commutativity is consistent with the rule because reversing the order of the vectors in the cross product reverses which direction the fingers curl, which flips the thumb to the opposite side.

questions.question: Construct a single equation involving force F, mass m, velocity v, and time t that is dimensionally consistent, and verify the consistency.
questions.answer: Sample answer: F = m v / t. Check: [F] = M L T⁻²; [m v / t] = M · (L T⁻¹) / T = M L T⁻². Both sides have dimensions M L T⁻², so the equation is dimensionally consistent. (Physically, F = Δ(mv)/Δt = rate of change of momentum, which is Newton's second law.) Other valid answers: F = m a (with a = v/t), F t = m v (impulse equals change in momentum), etc.

questions.question: Invent two vectors of magnitude 5 each whose sum has magnitude 5, and verify by computation.
questions.answer: Sample answer: take \vec{a} = 5 î and \vec{b} = (−5/2) î + (5√3/2) ĵ. Magnitude of \vec{a} = 5. Magnitude of \vec{b} = √(25/4 + 75/4) = √25 = 5. Sum: \vec{a} + \vec{b} = (5 − 5/2)î + (5√3/2)ĵ = (5/2)î + (5√3/2)ĵ. |\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = √(25/4 + 75/4) = √25 = 5. ✓. (The two vectors have a 120° angle between them; for any two equal-magnitude vectors with angle 120°, the sum has the same magnitude.)

questions.question: Devise a real-world example in which dimensional analysis is genuinely useful for predicting a relationship, and use it to predict the form (up to a dimensionless constant) of the relationship.
questions.answer: Sample example — terminal velocity of a small sphere falling slowly through a viscous fluid. Suppose the terminal velocity v_t depends on the sphere's radius r, the dynamic viscosity η of the fluid (dimensions M L⁻¹ T⁻¹), the density difference Δρ between sphere and fluid (M L⁻³) and the gravitational acceleration g (L T⁻²). Assume v_t = k r^a η^b (Δρ)^c g^d. Equate dimensions of v_t = LT⁻¹ with the RHS: L: a + (−b) + (−3c) + d = 1. T: −b − 2d = −1. M: b + c = 0. Solving: b = −1, c = +1, d = +1, a = +2. So v_t ∝ r² Δρ g / η. The actual physics (Stokes' law) gives the dimensionless constant: v_t = (2/9) r² Δρ g / η. Dimensional analysis alone fixed the functional form except for the 2/9 factor, which falls out of solving the Navier–Stokes equation. (Other valid examples: dependence of orbital period on planet mass and radius, dependence of frequency of a string on its tension and length, etc.)
